hero.name: Bhavna
hero.who: a homemaker in Ahmedabad who keeps saying yes to things she never wanted

story.b: Bhavna is cleaning the storeroom of her flat in Satellite, Ahmedabad, when she finds the evidence. A foot massager still in its box. Three jars of face cream from a door-to-door seller. A second pressure cooker. An extended warranty card for a mixer that broke anyway. A membership card for a gym she visited twice. She sits on the floor among the boxes and adds up the cost on her phone. It is more than a semester of her son Parth's college fees. She is careful with money in other ways. She bargains at the vegetable market and puts a little into an FD every Diwali. So why does she keep saying yes? She honestly cannot remember deciding to buy any of it.

ask.q: Bhavna is careful with money but keeps buying things she did not want. What is the most useful thing for her to understand?
o: That she is simply weak and should never go shopping
That sellers often trigger quick mental shortcuts, which she can learn to spot
That everything she bought was secretly a good deal
ask.why: Calling herself weak does not explain why a careful person keeps saying yes, and pretending the purchases were good deals avoids the lesson. Many yeses come from automatic shortcuts that sellers know how to press. Once she can name them, she can pause.

chapters.take: Many yeses are not decisions. They are shortcuts someone else pressed.

story.h: Free chaas at the saree shop
story.b: Bhavna goes to a saree shop near Ratan Pol to buy a simple cotton saree for her niece's school function. The owner is warm. He sends a boy for chilled chaas, gives her a small saree pin as a gift, and spends half an hour unfolding silks she never asked to see. By the end, Bhavna feels she owes him something. A voice in her head says she cannot leave with only a cheap saree after all this. She is reaching for her purse to buy a silk one costing eight thousand rupees when she stops. She asks herself whether she would buy it if the chaas and the pin had never happened. The answer is no. She buys the cotton saree, thanks him warmly and leaves.

ask.q: A builder's agent offers Bhavna's family a free lunch at a new housing site, then asks for a booking amount. What should they do?
o: Enjoy the lunch, but judge the flat as if it never happened
Pay a small booking amount to return the favour politely
Refuse all free things forever so nobody can pressure them
ask.why: A free gift creates a strong urge to give something back, even when nobody asked for it. Paying to return a lunch lets that urge make a huge decision. Refusing everything is unnecessary. Judging the offer on its own merits keeps the choice theirs.

chapters.take: A small favour can pull a big yes. Judge the offer without the gift.

story.b: Bhavna checks her bank messages and finds that a cooking app has been taking nine hundred and ninety-nine rupees every month. It started with a one-rupee trial. Then she filled in her food likes, made a profile and saved forty recipes. By then cancelling felt like undoing her own effort. She notices how one tiny yes made each next yes easier. She cancels it that afternoon. Then she wonders whether the same pull could help her. She has wanted to walk every morning for years. So she tells her sister Hetal and the neighbours on the building group that she will be at Vastrapur Lake at six every day. On cold mornings, she goes, partly because she said she would.

ask.q: Bhavna's son Parth wants to learn guitar but keeps putting it off. How could the same pull help him?
o: Sign up for an expensive course and hope the cost forces him
Keep the goal secret so there is no pressure if he quits
Tell friends he will practise every evening and share a short clip each week
ask.why: Once we say something out loud, we feel pressure to stay consistent with it. Keeping it secret removes that helpful pull, and an expensive course can become one more thing he regrets. A public promise with small regular check-ins turns the pull into support.

chapters.take: Small first yeses lead to bigger ones. Use that pull on purpose.

story.b: Bhavna's old mixer finally gives up, and she searches online for a new one. One brand has five thousand reviews, almost all five stars. Her hand moves toward the buy button. Then she reads a few. Many are two words long. Several say exactly the same thing. Lots were posted on the same two days. A smaller brand has fewer reviews, but they are long and mixed, with photos and complaints about the lid. She calls her neighbour Mrs Patel, who has used the smaller brand for three years and says it is solid. Bhavna buys that one. The same week, she notices a crowded new chaat stall near her building and realises the crowd is mostly the owner's cousins.

ask.q: Everyone in Bhavna's family group is sharing a new investment app, saying all their friends are earning on it. What should she do?
o: Check who is behind it and what it really does before following the crowd
Join quickly, since so many people cannot all be wrong
Wait to see how many more relatives join first
ask.why: Following what others do is a useful shortcut, but crowds can be staged or simply uninformed. More relatives joining is still just more crowd. Checking the facts and asking whether the crowd actually knows better protects her money.

chapters.take: A crowd is a clue, not proof. Ask if it actually knows better.

story.b: A young insurance agent visits Bhavna's flat with a leather folder and a smart blazer. Within five minutes she learns he grew up two lanes from her parents' old house in Bhavnagar. He speaks with the same accent as her father, praises her thepla and calls her ben. She likes him immediately. He opens his folder full of charts and says many senior professionals have taken this plan. Bhavna feels her trust warming fast, and she notices it. She asks herself one question. Do I like this policy, or do I like this boy? She asks him to leave the papers. That evening, she and her husband Nilesh read them slowly and check with an advisor they trust. The plan does not suit them at all.

ask.q: A man in a white coat sells health drinks at a mall, and Bhavna's sister feels sure they must be good. What should she ask?
o: Whether he is friendly and seems to care
Whether the product itself makes sense, apart from the coat and the charm
Whether other shoppers are already buying
ask.why: A uniform, a title or a warm manner makes us trust quickly, and friendliness says nothing about the product. Checking what other shoppers do just swaps one shortcut for another. Separating the person from the offer lets her judge what is actually being sold.

chapters.take: Separate the person from the offer. Like him, but judge the deal.

story.b: The big Diwali sale goes live on Bhavna's phone. A smart TV is heavily discounted, with a red timer counting down from fourteen minutes and a small line saying only two left. Her heart starts racing. Nilesh has been talking about a bigger TV for months. Her thumb hovers over the button. Then she recognises the rush, the same rush she felt before buying the foot massager. She closes the app and sets a reminder for the next morning. Over breakfast, they talk about whether they actually want a new TV. The old one works fine, and they would rather save for Parth's college trip. The next week, she sees the same TV at the same price, still with only two left.

ask.q: Bhavna's friend sees a flat booking scheme closing tonight, with only three units left. What would Bhavna tell her?
o: Book now, because such chances rarely come back
Book one and cancel later if needed
Slow down, and ask whether she would still want it without the deadline
ask.why: Deadlines and limited stock make us act fast and think less, which is exactly when big mistakes happen. Booking to cancel later may cost money and add pressure. Pausing and asking whether she would want it without the rush puts the decision back in her hands.

chapters.take: When something feels rare and urgent, slow down. Ask if you would want it anyway.

story.b: Months later, the storeroom in Bhavna's flat has space again. She sold the foot massager to a neighbour and gave the extra pressure cooker to Kokila ben, who helps in the house. Nothing new has come in that she did not truly decide on. She still enjoys chaas at the saree shop, and she still smiles at friendly salesmen. She simply pauses now. She sleeps on anything with a timer, reads reviews with one eyebrow raised and asks herself whether she likes the offer or the person. The walking habit at Vastrapur Lake has lasted all winter. One afternoon, her sister Hetal calls about a limited-time deal on gold coins. Bhavna laughs and tells her to call back tomorrow.

chapters.take: She still says yes often. Now the yes is actually hers.
